categories: ["ปัญหาเส้นเอ็นและเอ็น", "ปัญหาข้อศอก"]
synonyms: ["Epitrochleitis", "Medial Epicondylitis", "Inner Elbow Pain", "Sore Inner Elbow", "Sore Elbow Inside", "Interior Elbow Pain", "Elbow Pain Inside Of Elbow", "Epicondylitis Medial", "Golfers Elbow Medial Epicondylitis"]
conventional_description: Golfer's elbow, or medial epicondylitis, is an overuse injury affecting the tendons that attach the forearm muscles to the bony bump on the inside of the elbow. These tendons control wrist flexion and gripping - motions repeated in golf, racket sports, throwing, and even daily activities like lifting or typing. The pain typically builds gradually, centered on the inner elbow, and may radiate down the forearm. Diagnosis is usually made through a physical exam and patient history; imaging is rarely needed.
conventional_treatments: Standard care starts with rest, ice, and over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications. Physical therapy to stretch and strengthen the forearm muscles is a cornerstone, often alongside bracing or taping. If pain persists, corticosteroid injections or platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections may be offered. Surgery is considered only after months of failed conservative treatment.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees golfer's elbow as a local manifestation of Qi and Blood stagnation in the channels that run through the inner elbow. The most common scenario is simple overuse: repetitive gripping and flexing jams the flow of Qi and Blood right at the tendon attachment, creating a fixed, stabbing pain. The longer this stagnation sits, the harder it is to clear, and the more the tissues stiffen and swell.
But stagnation rarely develops in isolation. If the elbow is already strained, it becomes a magnet for external pathogens - especially Cold and Dampness. These can invade the channels during cold, wet weather or after exposure to drafts, adding a deep, weather-sensitive ache to the picture. This is why some people's elbows are barometers for rain.
A third pathway involves deficiency. When the body's overall Qi is weak - from chronic fatigue, poor digestion, or illness - it can't push Blood through the tight elbow tissues. The result is a dull, persistent ache that worsens with use and doesn't fully resolve with rest. Here, the stagnation is a consequence of not enough energy to move things, not just a traffic jam.
Less often, Dampness and Heat combine, especially in people who eat a lot of greasy, spicy, or alcoholic foods. The elbow can become red, warm, and swollen, with a pain that feels better with cold. Recognizing which pattern is dominant - stagnation, cold-damp, deficiency, or damp-heat - is what guides treatment.
classical_quote: 「风寒湿三气杂至，合而为痹也。」
classical_translation: "When the three Qi of wind, cold, and dampness arrive together, they combine to form Bi (painful obstruction) syndrome."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen  ,  Chapter 43 (Bi Lun) 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner starts by asking what the pain feels like and when it strikes. The most common pattern, Qi and Blood Stagnation, produces a fixed, stabbing or boring pain right over the inner elbow bone, often with visible swelling and tenderness. It worsens with continued use and eases with rest; the tongue may look dark or have purple spots, and the pulse feels wiry or choppy.
If the pain is worse in cold or damp weather and the elbow feels heavy or stiff, Painful Obstruction with Wind-Cold-Damp is more likely. The tongue is often pale with a white coating, and the pulse is tight or deep. This pattern arises when external factors invade an already overused joint.
When the pain is a dull ache that persists at rest and is accompanied by noticeable arm weakness and fatigue, the practitioner considers Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation. This chronic pattern is worse after exertion and often flares at night; the tongue is pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is weak and thready.
Less commonly, if the elbow is not just painful but also feels warm, looks red, and is more swollen than in other types, Damp Heat in the channels may be the culprit. This pattern is aggravated by hot, humid weather or rich, greasy foods. The tongue appears red with a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid or slippery.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pain at the inner elbow", "Swelling and pinpoint tenderness at the medial epicondyle", "Pain worsens with pressure and use of the arm", "Irritability or a feeling of tightness in the chest"]
patterns.worse_with: Overuse or repetitive arm movements, Cold or damp weather, Pressing on the tender spot, Stress and frustration
patterns.better_with: Resting the arm, Applying heat or warm compresses, Gentle stretching and movement, Warm, cooked, nourishing meals
patterns.why_this_happens: Repetitive overuse of the forearm flexor tendons - gripping, lifting, twisting - causes the local Qi to jam and the Blood to pool. When Qi cannot push Blood through the tight tissues, the inner elbow becomes a site of fixed, stabbing pain, swelling, and pinpoint tenderness. The longer the stagnation sits, the sharper the pain becomes, especially with pressure or use of the arm.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dark body with stasis spots and distended sublingual veins. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Rest and heat help move stagnant Qi and Blood, reducing the localized stasis that causes the stabbing pain. Cold and overuse further congeal Blood and tighten the tendons, worsening the blockage. Emotional stress aggravates Liver Qi stagnation, which is often the root of Blood stasis, so calming the mind supports healing.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest the elbow and avoid repetitive gripping or lifting until the sharp pain subsides. Apply warm compresses or a heating pad to promote circulation. Gentle stretching of the forearm flexors can help, but stop if pain sharpens. Eat warming, Blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, and dark leafy greens, and avoid cold, raw foods or excessive dairy, which can congeal Blood and worsen stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the elbow is already strained from overuse, it becomes vulnerable to external Wind, Cold, and Dampness. These pathogens invade the channels and settle in the joint, blocking the flow of Qi and Blood. The result is a deep, aching pain that stiffens the elbow and feels worse in cold or damp weather, as if the joint is being constricted from within.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, slightly swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating. Pulse: wiry and tight, or soggy and slow if Dampness predominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are the main culprits in this pattern; they constrict the channels and thicken the fluids that nourish the sinews, causing pain and stiffness. Warmth and gentle movement disperse the cold and damp, restoring circulation to the elbow. Rest allows the strained tissues to heal, while cold weather and raw foods introduce more cold and dampness, directly worsening the obstruction.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the elbow warm and protected from drafts and dampness. Gentle, slow stretching of the forearm muscles can help maintain mobility, but avoid overuse. Eat warming, cooked foods like soups and stews with ginger, and steer clear of cold, raw foods and icy drinks that can worsen internal dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens:
In golfer's elbow, when the body's vital energy (Qi) is weak-often from chronic overwork, poor diet, or constitutional factors-it fails to push blood through the tendons and channels of the inner elbow. Without enough Qi to keep blood moving, stagnation develops, causing a persistent dull ache and weakness in the forearm.
This stagnation is not from a sudden injury but from a gradual buildup of sludge-like blood that can't be cleared. The pain is fixed and deep, and it worsens with fatigue because the Qi is even less able to circulate. Night pain is common because blood flow naturally slows when the body is at rest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body with a dark or purplish tinge, possible stasis spots, teeth marks, thin white coat. Pulse: deep, fine, and choppy (rough, uneven).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi is the body's engine for moving blood. When Qi is deficient, blood easily stagnates, so rest and gentle movement keep blood flowing without draining Qi, while fatigue and overexertion deplete Qi further. Cold contracts the channels and slows circulation, worsening stagnation, whereas warmth relaxes the channels and promotes blood flow. Warm, easily digested foods strengthen the Spleen to produce more Qi, while raw, cold foods weaken it.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews to support Spleen Qi; avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken digestion. Gentle daily movement such as walking or Tai Chi helps Qi and Blood circulate without straining the elbow. Apply a warm compress to the inner elbow to ease stiffness and pain.

patterns.symptoms: ["Pain with local redness and heat at the inner elbow", "Swelling that is hot to the touch", "Pain relieved by cold compresses, aggravated by warmth", "Heavy, aching sensation in the forearm", "Thirst with desire to drink, irritability"]

patterns.why_this_happens: When external Damp-Heat invades the body - often in hot, humid weather - or when a diet rich in greasy, spicy, or alcoholic foods creates internal Damp-Heat, these pathogenic factors can settle into the elbow channels. The Heat causes redness, swelling, and a burning pain, while the Dampness makes the area feel heavy, stiff, and sluggish. Together they obstruct the flow of Qi and Blood at the medial epicondyle, producing the classic hot, swollen, and acutely tender elbow of this pattern.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is a combination of pathogenic moisture and warmth. Heat aggravates the inflammatory burning pain, while Dampness causes the heavy, swollen sensation. Cold compresses and cool environments counteract the heat, and dry weather or light diet reduce the dampness. Overuse generates friction and heat, and alcohol or greasy food directly add to the Damp-Heat burden, so avoiding them helps the channels clear and the elbow heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid alcohol, deep-fried foods, and spicy dishes that fuel Damp-Heat. Eat more cooling, light foods like cucumber, mung beans, and celery. Keep the elbow cool but not iced for long periods; gentle range-of-motion exercises prevent stiffness without overheating the joint.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture hurt for golfer's elbow?
faqs.answer: Most people feel a quick, mild pinch as the needle enters, followed by a dull ache, warmth, or a spreading sensation around the elbow - that's the Qi arriving, and it's a good sign. The needles used are hair-thin, and the treatment is generally very tolerable. Your practitioner may also use electro-acupuncture or moxibustion (gentle heat) to enhance comfort and effectiveness.

faqs.question: How long until I see results from TCM?
faqs.answer: Many patients feel some pain relief after the first few sessions, but real, lasting change takes time. For excess patterns like simple stagnation, you might see significant improvement in 3-4 weeks. If your pain is rooted in a deficiency, expect a slower, steadier climb - often 6-12 weeks to feel truly stronger. Consistency with herbs and home care makes a big difference.

faqs.question: Can I still play golf or work out during treatment?
faqs.answer: You'll need to modify activity, not necessarily stop entirely. The key is to avoid the specific movements that trigger your pain - heavy gripping, repetitive wrist flexion, or lifting with the palm up. Your practitioner will guide you on what's safe. Continuing to push through pain can undo the progress of treatment. Gentle stretching and non-aggravating movement are usually encouraged.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with physical therapy or medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM works well alongside physical therapy, and many patients do both. Just make sure your TCM practitioner and physical therapist know about each other's treatments. If you're taking anti-inflammatory or blood-thinning medications, tell your TCM practitioner - some herbs can interact with these. Never stop prescribed medications without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Will the pain come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to resolve the root imbalance, not just mask pain. If you complete treatment and address the underlying pattern - whether it's chronic cold-damp, Qi deficiency, or dietary damp-heat - recurrence is much less likely. However, returning to the same overuse patterns without proper conditioning or ergonomic changes can re-trigger the problem, just as with any treatment approach.

faqs.question: Are there any side effects from the herbs?
faqs.answer: Herbal formulas are generally well-tolerated when prescribed by a qualified practitioner. Some people may experience mild digestive changes initially, which usually settle. Because formulas are customized to your pattern, side effects are minimal. Always inform your practitioner of any medications or supplements you're taking to avoid interactions.

research.title: Acupuncture for the alleviation of lateral epicondyle pain: a systematic review
research.description: This systematic review found that acupuncture was effective in relieving lateral epicondyle pain in the short term compared to placebo, but the evidence was limited by small sample sizes and methodological flaws. While focused on lateral epicondylitis, the findings are relevant to medial epicondylitis due to similar pathophysiology.
research.periodical: Trinh KV, Phillips SD, Ho E, Damsma K. Acupuncture for the alleviation of lateral epicondyle pain: a systematic review. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2004 Sep;43(9):1085-90.
